turns.text: Turn the clock back to 2023. What problem was ESMFold actually trying to solve?

High-accuracy protein structure prediction had made a major leap, but many pipelines still depended on computationally expensive searches for evolutionary relatives. ESMFold explored whether a large protein language model could internalize enough evolutionary information to predict structure directly from one sequence.
That sounds like a promising direction. What mechanism actually makes it work?

ESM-2 learns contextual representations from large protein sequence databases, and a folding trunk converts those representations into three-dimensional coordinates and confidence estimates. Removing the multiple-sequence-alignment stage trades some peak accuracy for dramatically higher throughput and a simpler single-sequence workflow.
Why did the idea outlive one paper or experiment? What did later researchers actually inherit?

Experts generally treat ESMFold as strong evidence that protein language models learn structural information at useful biological scale. Its lasting contribution is not only a fast predictor but also a demonstration that language-model representations can support massive structure atlases and downstream protein analysis.
ESMFold mattered not only as a result, but as a method that later researchers could test, adapt, and extend.
